utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. It is unfortunate, but it was necessary for us to start late because the previous Trial Chamber ran overtime. We are now ready to get underway with the next witness. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness is Mr. Lufti Ramadani, and he will be led in chief by Ms. Tove Nilsen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lutfi --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Lutfi Ramadani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber mention for counsel that the practice we would like followed with any witness that is to be -- have the advantage of Rule 92 bis or Rule 92 ter, that when the statement is tendered, a short summary of its contents, shorter in the case of Rule 92 ter than Rule 92 bis, should be read by counsel into the record. This then enables, in particular, members of the public who are here and those who are following proceedings more remotely to have at least a very brief understanding of the nature of the evidence which the witness has given and which is set out in the statement of the witness's evidence which is tendered, so that in particular for Rule 92 bis, but less extensively for Rule 92 ter, counsel should be prepared with a short summary of the essential points of the evidence of the witness. Now, it may be that that having been announced today, it will not be feasible to be introduced today. We will see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may ask one question before we proceed. Should the summary be done in the presence of the witness or before the witness comes to the well of the court to testify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It should be done in the presence of the witness because in the case of 92 bis, unless the witness is here for cross-examination, there will be no witness. In the case of Rule 92 ter, a statement is not tendered until the witness has identified it and confirmed its correctness. So inevitably, the witness will need to be here for the purposes of 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is the witness available?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Nilsen. I beg your pardon. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation which is on the card that has been handed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Ms. Nilsen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Witness Lutfi Ramadani will testify about allegations in paragraph 72 A and I, paragraph 75 C, and paragraph 77, Schedule C, in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Before I go ahead and read the summary of Mr. Ramadani's previous testimony in court, I will ask him a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ramadani.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were born in the municipality of Suva Reka, the 20th of March, 1944?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you are a Muslim of Albanian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you are residing in Krushe e Vogel, or the Serbian name of the village, Mala Krusa, where you have lived since 1958?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, at Krusha e Vogel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: You have lived there since 1958; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I would also like you to confirm whether you are married and have two surviving sons.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Is it also correct that two of your sons died the 26th of March, 1999, Mr. Ramadani?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Ramadani, do you recall that you gave a testimony as a witness in court before this Tribunal last time in September 2006?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Did this testimony reflect what happened to you and your neighbours and your family and the village Krusha e Vogel in March 1999? Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And did you, Mr. Ramadani, have the opportunity to read through this testimony before you came here today?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, I did read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today that you had given last time you testified in court, would you give the same answers today?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender 65 ter 05104, which is the transcript of Mr. Ramadani's testimony given the 28th and the 29th of September, 2006, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00306, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In which trial was that given?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: That was given in the trial of Milutinovic et al, the Mos, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And then, Your Honours, I would like to give a short summary of the witness's testimony from September 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Nilsen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: The witness describes that in -- the 25th of March, 1999, his family left their house and they hid in the woods as the Serb police had surrounded and commenced shelling the village Krusha e Vogel. They started to burn the Albanian houses. He explained in court that he and his family and several hundred other people spent the night in the house of Sejdi Batusha. There were approximately 500 together, the night from 25th to 26th of March. He explained that two other families remained in the woods. The witness describes in his previous testimony that the Serbs were wearing camouflage uniforms, black and blue police uniforms, and that he also saw tanks and so-called APCs positioned around the village. The witness will further -- or he further explained that the group of people that was gathered in Sejdi Batusha's house was ordered from the yard onto the road outside this house the next day, the 26th, in the morning, and then the men were separated from the women. The younger boys from 13, 14 age had to stay with the men. The women were ordered to go to Lake Vermacija [phoen] - excuse me if I'm not pronouncing it correct - after being forced to hand over their personal belongings. The remaining men who the been separated from their women were then forced to line up in columns, and they were taken down the road into a cow-shed, a hay barn, which belonged to Qazim Batusha. When they came into this cow-shed, a policeman arrived and he was carrying a big machine-gun, and he told his colleagues that, I will take care of this, or similar. The Serbs with the machine-gun appeared in the doorway and fired upon them. The witness fell on the ground together with all the other who were gathered in this barn, and there were over a hundred together. A lot of men fell on top of him. The witness described in his previous testimony that when the machine-gun stopped, when the person who fired ran out of bullets, he heard the sound of single shots, and he described it as whoever who could raise his head after this machine-gun shooting were being finished with single shots. The witness then described that he could hear the sound of burning and that the cow-shed starting to burn. The witness also described that the crippled villager, a man who was confined to a wheelchair, Sait Hajdari, was positioned in the doorway of the cow-shed, and the witness had physically to move him from the doorway in order to be able to escape, which he managed. He will also explain, and he explained in his testimony, that according to him, six people together managed to get out of this burning barn, this burning cow-shed, while there were men laying around them dead, covered in blood, and the barn was burning. The witness told that when he managed to get out of the barn, he started to run and he started his escape. Outside the barn, he saw several policemen talking to each other on the road outside this barn, and he explained that he recognised some of them. He explained that these people he recognised were Stankovic Bosko, Sejko [phoen] Stankovic, Stanko Nikolic, Rade Nikolic, and Cvetkovic Bosko. The witness also described that while he managed to escape from the bullets and the fire, amongst the killed people were his two sons, his brother, and his nephew; and his youngest son was 14 years old. The witness will then describe -- or he described his escape route from the burning hay barn along the road where they were shot at because they were discovered by the Serbs. He explained how he fled into the stream and then up into the forest where he remained for several days. He described also that he could smell a terrible smell from the burned body in the village during his stay in this forest. The witness made a list in 1999 of the men that as to here -- as to his knowledge lost their lives during this event, and he confirmed that this list was the correct one last time he testified for the Tribunal. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That statement is -- that previous transcript of evidence has been received as Exhibit P306. Is there anything further, Ms. Nilsen?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Not from the summary, Your Honours. Thank you. I will -- I have several questions to the -- to the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I am aware that we have already put up a map of Krusha e Vogel, Kosovo, during testimony of the previous witness, but I would like to have a brief look at an unmarked map, also, for this witness. So may I please have 65 ter number 00615 put up on the screen, page 22. If we could zoom in a little bit on the area of -- a little bit more. Is that possible? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, I know this is -- it's not very easy to read on this map, but are you able to find your village Krusha e Vogel on the map? Could you please point at it, please?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I cannot see very well. This is Prizren, and that is the road that should normally lead to Krusha e Vogel. I -- my eyesight is not quite up to the point, and I cannot discern it very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Could we have the witness to mark it on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He can't mark because he says he can't discern the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Yes, if it's possible to zoom it a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take the other pair of glasses.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I just ask you to mark --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: That's Prizren, right? It should be round about here. I can't notice the letters. They are way too small. I'm not able to -- to work out what it is. This is Prizren. This is Gjakova. It should be round about in that area. That's the road that leads to Rahovec. If you are able to zoom in so that I could see the letters properly, I'd be able to mark it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Is there any other map you can show me?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]... not, Mr. Ramadani, but ...

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I think there must be another map which I have seen before.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Yes. That might be correct, Mr. Ramadani, but I think you --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: In -- the map that I myself have compiled is much clearer than this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: But this is better with -- with unmarked -- are you able to see Krusha e Vogel from here, Mr. Ramadani? If not, we'll just ...

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]... It's not very crucial importance, so I think that we can just skip it if you can't see it.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I don't think I'm able to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I can't see it. I can't see it with my naked eye. My eyesight is not that strong.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I will go on, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, if you can tell the Court, prior to March 1999, approximately how was the ethnic distribution in the village Krusha e Vogel? How many houses, approximately, were Albanian, and how many were Serbian?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were 70 Albanian households in Krusha e Vogel. Thirty households were Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. How as far to your knowledge did the different ethnics co-exist before March 1999?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There was no problem whatsoever between the Albanians and the Serbs. There was nothing wrong in the relations between the Serbs and the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to go to the transcript, page 6. Exhibit 00306.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: You have told previously that you were more than 500 people who fled into the woods the 25th and that you heard firing from the village that you had fled from. What happened to the people who remained in the woods and those who did not spend the night at Sejdi Batusha's house, Mr. Ramadani?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They spent the night in the woods up until the very morning. They had something to eat. They had something to eat, and they were able to survive the night. They were able to listen to what was happening, but they spent the night there in that little creek, around that little creek.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Do you know how many there were?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Eight people, two families.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Can you mention the surname of these two families?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Liman Hazeri with his wife and their son Avdyl, his brother Nebi, Nebi's wife, and Luan. There were two others who were also in the same company, two children. Avdyl was the one who was disabled, and that is why it was impossible to move him. They carried him on the 26th to get him to where the rest of the population was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened with the people who spent the night in Sejdi Batusha's house? What happened the next morning? What did you observe?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: On the evening of the 25th, we went there because it was very, very cold. There were elderly people, women who had given birth two or three days earlier, and that is the reason why we headed toward Sejdi Batusha's house, where we spent the night. When we woke up on the 26th in the morning, almost the entire population that was there emerged into the courtyard. That is at about 7.00 in the morning. We just observed and listened to what was happening on the outskirts of the village. However, on the 25th and the 26th, shelling resumed on the part of the Serbs of that village, as well as the policemen and the others who had come to their aid. They started setting fire to the houses of the Albanians. Initially they went to the houses to carry out their looting, after which they set fire to the houses. They brought trucks. They filled them up. As soon as the trucks and lorries were on their way, they set fire to the villages, and the fire was approaching the population. At the same time, Isen Kanjusha was killed in his own courtyard by the Serbs and --

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I'll stop you there.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: -- the police were in the vicinity. Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Sorry. You said the policemen and the others. Who are these others that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were the Serbs from the same village. Some had their uniforms on; some were in civilian clothing. There were others, as well, policemen in uniform who had come all the way from Prizren or from elsewhere. I'm not sure. So they kept approaching the population while setting fire to the properties, and when they approached to Milaim Batusha's house, which is adjacent to Sejdi Batusha's house - I can show that on the map if need be - and then they -- in fact, we -- we were beginning to get scared because they started removing some tiles from the houses and shooting from there. On Milaim Batusha's house, they just opened the windows on the first floor and put the automatic rifles through, and they observed us. When the women saw that had they killed Isen, some of them -- some from amongst the women started fainting. There were quite a few who went to fetch some water when they heard from the windows the order not to move, not to go to fetch any water on pain of death, which meant that nobody was able to move, and we had to stand still.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: And we only used the water that was available to pour onto their faces.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Okay. I want to know, when you were inside Sejdi Batusha's house, did you have any discussion with each other, what to do? Did you hear about any arrangements that had been made previously that maybe affected on what you did next?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Others were involved in -- in talking what to do. I wasn't involved. We heard that there was some sort of talks between Albanians and Serbs, but I myself was not personally present, and I don't know what happened. I think there was some elderly gentlemen who were involved. They have since departed. But I personally am not aware of what kind of what kind of talks they had. Whatever agreement they were able to reach, however, was never -- was never observed by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please describe what happened next? You are -- you have already told that you saw a man being killed, and you named this person. Can you please mention it again?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Isen Kanjusha, who was killed in his own courtyard, which is adjacent to the house of Sejdi Batusha. We were able to see him being killed from the courtyard of Sejdi Batusha's house, and that is the reason why women and men and everybody got scared. Police came and established themselves in Milaim's house, which added to the fear amongst the children and the women and the men that were over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. At some stage, you were gathered together with the people who had spent the night in the woods. In which way did this happen? How were you gathered together, and can you please tell the Court what happening then when you are there together in the yard?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Do you mean what we were in that courtyard or when we were in the woods?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I mean when you were in this courtyard and the people from the woods afterwards gathered together with you.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Okay. I understand it now. When we were ordered not to move to go and fetch water, they called for a volunteer to go to them. Aziz Shehu went, and he was ordered -- he was given ten minutes to go and summon the people who were up in the mountains to come down. Aziz went. As I said, it was Liman Hazeri, and they carried Avdyl and brought him to join the rest of the people there, and as soon as that happened we were ordered to move out of the courtyard and onto the road but to leave everything behind, clothes, everything, and just go out into the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please describe, Mr. Ramadani, who these people were that was giving you and the other women, everyone these orders? Can you describe them?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Policemen. They were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And can you just describe briefly their uniforms, how you were seeing them? Were they wearing weapons, and which kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Blue uniforms, while their weapons -- they had automatic weapons and pistols and knives, everything that the policemen usually have as weapons. There, all of them were policemen, while the army, they were along the asphalt road and on the hills.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you were then separated from the women and brought to this barn, the cow-shed, do you remember anything from the walk down the road, who you were walking next to and what you saw?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We remained on the road for some time until they separated the men from the women. They told the women to leave in the direction to the left and told us to go in the direction to the right. The women set off. Cvetkovic Djordje, a policeman, ordered two other policemen to go and fetch the other children who were up to the age of 13 and bring them where the men were. So these two policemen went to get the children, but the women couldn't let their children go. They started to use force. The women started screaming and yelling, and they told them to shut up and threatened to kill them all. So they asked them, What are we supposed to do now? You took our men. You took our children. And they said to them, You can go and drown yourself in the Drini River or you can go to Albania. You make your choice. So after they separated the women, we were told to kneel down and to put our hands over our heads. We stayed in that position for some time. Then some policemen came. They were dressed in uniforms and wore balaklavas. They maltreated us for some time. We remained there for some time again. They took all our money and documents. They told us to empty our pockets. They told Adem Jusufi to collect all the items that we took from our pockets and bring them to one of the policemen. So then they ordered us to stand up and to form columns of three and to walk along the road. When they went to take the children from the women, my young son, who was 13, was one who was brought in. So we were walking along the road, and when we arrived at Qazim Batusha's house they ordered us to stop. They took us directly to the barn. This barn had walls, concrete blocks. There was fodder for the cattle there. The owner used to keep the cattle inside there in the past, but he didn't at the time when we were taken in.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I would like to put up 65 ter 00099. It's aerial photographs of Mala Krusa.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, do you recognise the village of this picture?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Now I can see it better on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Is it hard to see the details? If you like, we have a -- another picture, but I would like you to describe the things you see here if you can. Can you see --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I can using this photograph or another photograph. There is no problem on my side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: We'll start with this first, Mr. Ramadani. Can you first please point out on the photograph the house where you lived, your house with your wife and your kids. Can you see this from this --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: This one here is my house. I marked it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Just leave it there. Yeah. And then if you can draw a circle around the house of Sejdi Batusha where you spent the night.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We were in the woods here. The woods are nearby, and this is Sejdi Batusha's house, these three houses which are a little bit up and this one here. There was another one, but it cannot be seen on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Please draw a circle around this house, Mr. Ramadani. Sejdi Batusha's house.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Shall I encircle all the houses that I mentioned, all his houses, or only the house where we were?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Only the house where you spent the night.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We were here in this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: In the big house there?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: And this is the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Is this the circle -- can you --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: So this is the house we were in, Sejdi Batusha's house. These other houses also belonged to Sejdi Batusha, but this one, that's where the men spent the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: And on the 26th, when we woke up we were here in the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Can you please also, Mr. Ramadani, point out the Court the area of the woods that you were hiding before you went to this Sejdi Batusha's house and spent the night, just a cross.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The woods should be somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: In the corner --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: And here is --

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: -- to the left.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: -- the little creek. You cannot see it on the photograph. It's a little bit further, but it's here in this direction where we stayed in the woods. There is creek there, quite a long one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: This is where we were on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]... between intervening, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There will need to be a general cross or a circle around the area of the woods, I would suggest, Ms. Nilsen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Could you please, Mr. Ramadani, draw a larger circle around Sejdi Batusha's house where you spent the night from the 25th to the 26th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: These are the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: But not all the houses. The house that you spent the --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I apologise. Here. This is the house. It's by the road, and here is a courtyard. This is the house. And this here is a courtyard, and that's where we went on the -- on that morning at 7.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: This is the road, the road that goes through the village and upwards. These are --

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: -- Ahmet and Zaim's house. They are Batusha family too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, are you able to see on the photograph the woods where you spent the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The wood is here. You cannot see all of it, but it starts from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you put a cross in the location that you're saying the woods --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's at the left-hand bottom of the photograph. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Here on the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like a plain here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you then -- you already pointed out to us where the courtyard is. So if you could please just draw a line from the courtyard to the cow-shed or the barn that you were brought to and a circle around the place where you mean that the barn is at the picture.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Can you please draw a circle around the barn that you were brought to, Mr. Ramadani.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: This is where they separated the men from the women, and here are Qazim's -- the gate to Qazim's house, and this is the location. Shall I mark it with a cross or encircle it?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: This is fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: If we could have the other picture up, please, page 2. Sorry, I would like to tender this 65 ter number as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before that is received, the area to which the men were taken in the witness's description and which he says was then the site of a barn or a cow-shed is very close to the centre of the photograph but toward the lower edge of the photograph, and it is marked with two or three overlapping red circles, and there is a line joining it from the courtyard of Sejdi Batusha, that line mostly following the roadway which passes through the village. The photograph as marked will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00307, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And then if I could please have the next picture, page number 2 in the same 65 ter number shown at the screen. 00099, page 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Here we just see the same area from another angle. I would just like you to point out two things here, Mr. Ramadani.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: The house of Sejdi Batusha where you spent the night, a ring around that, and a cross where the barn was. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. My hand is trembling, I'm sorry. It's here. Sejdi Batusha's house is this one. And now, just a moment, for the barn. It's here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could you please, Mr. Ramadani, confirm whether there was a person confined to a wheelchair amongst the people who had to go inside the barn, who were forced inside the barn, a crippled man, and who was this?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: One hundred and nine men were forced into this location. There were two invalids, but the one with the wheelchair is Sait Hajdari. Avdyl was carried inside the barn, while the one who was in the wheelchair, he remained at the door. After a short time, the policemen came - it didn't take them that long - and they started to shoot inside the location. I saw a policeman who was wearing a helmet, who was wearing uniform, and others joined in in the shooting with automatic rifles, machine-guns, some from the windows, some from the door, and they were shooting at us. When they finished all the rounds, they came in and with their pistols, whoever would lift his head up, they would shoot them with a pistol. Later on, I didn't see how, but we were caught in fire. Everything was on fire, the bodies, the walls. So when the location was set on fire, my hand, this one got burned. My clothes were -- parts of them were burning because I was covered by other bodies. When I reached the door, Sait Hajdari was there in his wheelchair. I just pushed him a little bit so I could make a leave-way for me, and the room was filled with smoke and fire. I managed to came -- come out. There were people outside here, policemen and other people here on this road. I didn't have time to see who that was. I just escaped here to the left and through our houses. I left 103 men behind, four of them my family members, two of my sons, that is, and my brother and his son.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ramadani. Did you see any of the people who were shooting at you in the barn? Did you see it when they were starting, except for this one person that you told opened fire?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were others, the one with the machine-gun. You see, I was here in the corridor. The barn had two rooms and a corridor. I was in the corridor. This came to the main door that led to the corridor, while the others came from the windows, and that's how they were shooting inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: If I could please tender this photograph, also, as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will P00308, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And then if I could please have 65 ter 00100 up on the screen, please. That's already an exhibit number, sorry, so it's P00304, and it's the pictures that is shown from the previous witness of what is left of the Batusha barn. I'm not going to show all the pictures, but I would like to have page number 2 up at the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, do you recognise this place?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: What do you see at the picture?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Next to this one here was the barn, next to this house which is Bali Avdyli's house, and this small one here was like a summer kitchen or something like that, while the barn was here. The place was blown up in the air.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: If you would like the Court to see where you mean the barn was, please make a cross; otherwise, we're not able to see where you're pointing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Here, up to here in this direction. This is where the foundations were.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: That should be okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: This is the location that was blown up.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Could we please have page number 3 up at the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you want to tender this?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I would like to tender this. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00309, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And then page 3 from P00304.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, this is just the same area, but do you have anything to say in addition to what you said in the previous picture?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: This is where the incident occurred. They mined the place so that they can erase all the traces. They blew up the barn, and these are the leftovers of the concrete wall, and as a result of the explosion the house nearby was also damaged. You can see the foundations and the damaged walls. So this is the building -- the place where the building once stood and that was later on blown up.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: As this is already tendered, Your Honours, I would just go further to page number 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, the water you can see here, can you just describe what you're seeing?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is where one of the room was. As I said, there were two rooms and a corridor. This is one of the craters filled with water, and this is where the corridor was. As I said, the building was blown up. You have two craters filled with water. I guess when the photographs were taken, the water was there. This is the crater from one of the rooms, and this here is the corridor, and that there is the other room.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: "That there," is that where the water is now or where is -- if you could please put a cross to the place where you mean that the corridor was.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The corridor, yes, here. From here to here. And on this side is the room, and on the other side is the other room.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, you said "from here to here." Can you put another cross where you mean the corridor ends?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. Up to here. This is the corridor, and this is the door to the corridor. So on both sides of the corridor are the rooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Maybe when you are drawing now, maybe you could just, if you're able to, draw where you mean the rooms connected to the corridor were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've been told by the witness one of them is the crater that has water in it that we can see in the foreground, and he has marked at the moment just with a marking the position of the second room. I wonder, Mr. Ramadani, whether you would mind putting a number 3 where you say the second room was on the other side of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one here is also a room, and this one here is a corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ramadani. Can you please put a number 4 to the point in the corridor that you mean that you were positioned during this shooting.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: This is where you were standing?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. I was there at the corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And where did you escape? Did you escape from an entrance, or can you just show where you escaped with a number 5.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: All right. You mean how I left the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Just like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I guess --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: This was filled with bodies on all sides, so I crawled and walked over the bodies to get out.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I would like to tender this as an exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The last marking showing the doorway which the witness took to leave the corridor is marked by a line from the number 4 to the wall on the -- as one looks at the photograph, on the left-hand side, and there is a marking there meant to illustrate the doorway, and it is through that doorway the witness says that he left the corridor. With that explanation in the transcript, this marked photograph will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00310, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: If we then could go directly to 65 ter 00101. Thank you. If we can have both of the pictures at the same time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this wheelchair, Mr. Ramadani? It sounds like you do.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: This is Sait Hajdari's wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you recognise the woman next to the wheelchair?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. It's his wife, his wheelchair. It's Sait Hajdari's wife, even though I don't know her very well. I know it's her, but I recognise the wheelchair better because I had to push it away, away from the door. Sait was on his wheelchair, and I had to push him away to free the passage for myself. He was dead and burning at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: If I could also have this picture, this exhibit -- tender as an exhibit, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00311, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I have some few questions left for you, Mr. Ramadani. When you started your escape from the burning barn, did you see anyone alive before you escaped, inside the barn?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, I do, two or three boys. They were alive. They were asking, What should we do? And I told them, Whoever can should leave now. They -- some of them left, some towards the direction of that creek that can be seen on the photograph, and in fact they were executed there at the creek. There were two of them of 17 years' age. Once -- we left on the left-hand side, alongside the houses. I can show it on the photograph if need be. I saw these youngsters once the rest were dying at that stage. A hundred and three were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Did anyone escape together with you, Mr. Ramadani, or did you escape alone?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were two of us -- three. There was me, Agim Asllani, and Bajram Zylfiu. There were three of us. We left passing alongside the house, whilst the others, Petrit, Qamil, and the others went down towards the meadow. These were the two that survives, whilst the others two youths were the ones who were killed in the vicinity of the creek. They were asked to put -- they were asked to put their hands above their heads and were killed with no further ado. We were able to retrieve their bodies only after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember making a list of the names that you meant were deceased, that lost their lives inside the barn? Do you remember that you have provided this for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I have the list on me if you want it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: And it's the same list.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember when you made this list?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Immediately afterwards, before going to Albania, because I stayed roaming around the Krusha area for about five weeks. In fact, I spent about ten days roaming around mountains and creeks and so on and so forth. That is when I compiled that list. So I had it ready to produce to the investigators when they showed up.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And do you remember approximately when you handed it over to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I can't recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Was it before or after you left Albania? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Before leaving for Albania. I compiled the list before leaving for Albania, but I suffered quite a lot roaming around the mountains. I re-did that list in Albania once again, and I kept it with me all the time. I gave it to the investigators when they came to meet me. However, I don't know whether they brought this list here and tendered it here or whether they kept it for themselves, but I do have another list here on me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] We also have the list here. I just wanted you to tell the Court approximately --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Just like you to tell --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I have dated it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. But I would just like you to tell approximately when you mean that you handed it over. Was it before or after you left Albania? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Upon returning from Albania -- before leaving for Albania, I didn't have contact with anybody else. It was impossible. It was a war, wartime. There were lots of policemen roaming around. It's a very long story. It's a very long story to be told, including where I stayed, which road I took, how I was in hiding, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I gave them the list upon returning from Albania. Even my statements were given after returning from Albania, not during the war, because during that time I was roaming barefoot around the mountains. All -- because all the clothes that I had on were burned at the -- at that crime site.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: If I could please have 65 ter 02357 put on the screen. Thank you. It is a 4-page document, Your Honours, so it will be two pages at the same time. Yeah, well, this is the translated version of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Ramadani that -- is this the list? Do you recall this list?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. Shehu, Shehu, Shehu. There should be 39 Shehus. Maybe not 39, because 9 of them were the ones who were burned because they refused to leave their house, five brothers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: If we could go directly to -- or before we go to page 2, these are the names; you recognise them --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And go directly to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And this is number 22 to 65 -- 64, sorry. These are also -- when you have a brief look at them, these are also the names that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes. These are the names, including my children, Bajram, Afrim, Murat, Selajdin. These are my two children and Ramadani, all the Ramadanis.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Which number, Mr. Ramadani, are these deceased people that you mention now, your family? Which number on the list?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: 61. Murat is 58, Selajdin is 59, Bajrami is at 61, 14 years of age, 15. 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could turn directly to page 3. On this page, Mr. Ramadani, there is a handwritten name as -- visible as number 103. Is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, it is, because I had omitted one name which I've added in my own handwriting. This is a young boy. Yes. It is my handwriting, my own. The only thing missing over there is his age because I wasn't aware of what -- how old he was, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And was this name provided after you had given the list away to the investigators? When -- do you remember when you put this handwritten name on, approximately?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I did it at that time. This name ought to be in the very same list, but I can't be a hundred per cent certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: That's fine. If we then could go directly to page 4, the last page on this document.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: These are the names of those who survived. These were some of them who did not leave their own houses but who were burned inside their own houses. These are the main ones, Nikolic Dimitrije, Nikolic Ranko, Nikolic Momcilo, Sava, Zlatko, Ranko, Sveta, and Djordjevic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: There is also a number 9 there, which also is written -- handwritten name.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, Isnija. Isnija Rashkaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And this is your handwriting as well?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I forgot it. Yes, it is my own handwriting, because we were not able to find him. We found him later. We did not know whether he had been killed or burned or so on. We were only able to find his remains. He had been burned alongside the others, but some of his remains we were able to find. They were all people who burned to death.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I would like to tender this list, Your Honours, as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you discussed the names 1 to 8 who were in the third group on the page?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: He mentioned this group, Your Honours, but I can, of course, ask him once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: The last eight names, Mr. Ramadani, could you please describe to the Court what these names area since they are in a separate group?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: These are the names of the policemen. These were policemen who were in uniform. They had been in uniform and were well armed since 1993 -- or 1998, forgive me. All the Serbs of Kosova were uniformed like that, but Nikolic Dimitrije had had a coffee shop since 1999, which was later used as a police station. Police -- policemen were stationed there. He ran this coffee shop with his own two sons. They were all in police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Did you recognise these people during the events of the 25th and 26th at any stage? Were they people that you observed?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Very well. I saw them very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Nikolic Dimitrije, Nikolic Ranko, Nikolic Momcilo, they were all there. They were somewhere nearby. They did not join inside. They did not come to where the main concentration of the people were, but they stayed at a distance, all these three. There were others who I had -- I have noted down. These were the main ones, though. Nikolic Ranko was, I think, the main one of them. Dimitrije was the one who had the coffee shop. Nikolic Ranko, Nikolic Momcilo were regular policemen. Sava, again, a uniformed policemen with the regular police. Slatko Djordjevic, Petkovic Ranko, Tasic Sveta, Cvetkovic Djordje, they were all regular police officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ramadani. I just wonder where were you positioned when you were observing these men? Did you see them before you went into the barn or after you escaped, maybe even in the yard?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I saw them before being led into that cow-shed, but I saw them because they were moving just around, just in front of that cow-shed, and we could easily see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Did you know these people from before?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. They were my neighbours; very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: What did they wear? Did they wear uniforms, or were they in civilian clothes? Can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They were in uniform, all of them. There were others who were in civilian clothing who had red and blue armbands. They swapped them, those armbands. That wasn't important. I can -- I can -- this is the names that I've put on the list, and I'm able to show you where their houses were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You tendered the 4-page list; is that correct? It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00312, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: If I can also ask you, Mr. Ramadani, do you recall if you saw any outside the barn when you were escaping from the burning cow-shed or the burning barn? Did you see any of these people that you were mentioning, that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No. I wasn't able to do that because I was at a very long distance from them. I was in the woods, and so I wasn't able to discern from that distance who it was. I was only able to see people but not be able to tell who it was. They were the ones who took part. They did the shooting from the door, from the windows.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: These neighbours that you were talking about that you recognised -- that you recognised, were they belonging to the police, or what unit did they belong to and -- as to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They were members of the regular police.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Were they reservists?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No, the regular police. There were some youths who were members of the reserve forces, but these were the regular police. There were others who were members of the regular police, but these were the main ones, the ones who called the shots. So whenever something were to happen at Krusha e Vogel, they would bring some policemen to Krusha e Vogel, and whilst these ones would be taken from Krusha e Vogel and sent somewhere else on duty. I don't know where. But during those days on the 25th and 26th, they remained at Krusha e Vogel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: How are you able to say that they were part of the police, Mr. Ramadani? How could you be so sure about that? What makes you certain of that?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I'm certain not only because I saw them, but I was in contact with them. They have always been in police uniform. The Pinzgauer came to collect them, sometimes brought them back in the evening, sometimes it didn't, but they -- they were all -- always travelled in Pinzgauers or in APCs, in police APCs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And could you please just describe the uniforms that you used to -- to see them in?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Blue. Camouflage uniform, blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Did they always wear the same uniforms, or did they sometimes wear other colours, or can you say anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They always wore the same police uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have reached the point that we can't go any longer because the tape length, Ms. Nilsen, so we must now adjourn to enable the tapes to be rewound, and that is half an hour, and we will resume, then, at 25 minutes past 4.00. Now, we hope to be able to complete the evidence of this witness today, so I trust your examination is near an end.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I only have five or ten minutes left, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's the time that's needed for cross-examination that must be considered. We will now adjourn and resume at 25 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nilsen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have a few questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, you talked about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: You talked about the group of policemen, of local policemen. Did you know who was in charge of these local policemen, the group, your neighbours, your Serb neighbours?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I don't know who their commander was. They should know themselves. I don't know. At that stage, we were not aware who was their leader, but I simply know of the group around Dimitrije who had that coffee shop, and we know that the orders came from above to these policemen, and their command was headquartered in Prizren, not at Krusha e Vogel. So their high command was not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any knowledge to the commanders or the management who was the head of the local service that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know who the commander was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, Mr. Ramadani, I would like you to explain to the Court what you were doing for a living prior March 1999.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: A farmer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And are you still working as a farmer, Mr. Ramadani?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, I still do. Before March, even though we worked as farmers, we -- we couldn't even carry out that vocation because we couldn't even get the fuel. Police would not give us the necessary fuel to run our machinery.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have to ask you over again about the question regarding the -- the commander of the policemen. You said that they were headquartered in -- and then I think we missed the place where you talked about.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: As I said it earlier, Dimitrije Nikolic and his two sons had opened a coffee shop, and police used to come in Pinzgauers to that coffee shop and -- whilst they were mistreating people at Krusha e Vogel. The others who were at Krusha e Vogel were transported or taken away from Krusha e Vogel elsewhere, and I think that Dimitrije played the role of lead officer in that area. I think the orders came from elsewhere, but he had his own coffee shop, and I think that the other policemen acted on his orders. They went out on patrol. They mistreated children on their way to school. They pointed the barrels of their guns to -- at the children. They kept asking the children, What on earth are you after? Are you requesting the presence of NATO and America here? And they kept saying that -- saying high and low that they were going to kill every single Albanian. There came a point when children were unable to go to school following the regular route, and they had to go in a roundabout manner through creeks and mountains and so on. This coffee shop was in the very centre of the village, located in the very centre of the village, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, but just for the record, I think that the registrar missed it, but you said that the headquarter to these policemen in your village, that they had management, a commander higher up in another place, in another city. Could you just repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They came from Prizren. They came from Prizren on a Pinzgauer. They brought them on a Pinzgauer, and they took the other lot. They stayed there, eating, drinking, day and night. That place was full day and night. Some came down there. The other lot were taken away and deployed elsewhere. I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ramadani. My last question is -- to you is also for the record. Can you please tell me your full name and pronounce it. We're a little bit uncertain if it's Lufti or Lutfi. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Lutfi Ramadani, L-u-t-f-i.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nilsen. Mr. Djordjevic, do you have cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but to clarify some things that we heard today, I will be asking some questions in my cross-examination today to the witness that we have in front of us here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Ramadani. My name is Dragoljub Djordjevic. I'm an attorney-at-law, and I defend the accused in this case, Vlastimir Djordjevic. Mr. Ramadani, in your statement that was tendered into evidence under 92 ter by the Prosecution, and it was admitted in the Milutinovic case, you said quite a few things, and I will have to ask you some questions about them to get to the bottom of some things and to establish facts. First of all, as regards what you said that you had seen in the early morning on the 25th of March, 1999, you said that you saw Serb forces arriving, that you could hear sounds of various machinery, tanks, armoured vehicles, and so on. That's what you say in your statement. And then the people from the village, primarily those of Albanian ethnic background, went into the woods. Now, I will not ask for the aerial picture to be shown again because we all remember -- remember where you said the woods were, and you marked all the locations that are important and relevant for this case, but I will first ask you this question: What was the time when you headed into the woods, and what was specifically the reason that prompted you to go into the woods?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The reason why we went to the woods at around 4.00 in the morning - I didn't see my watch - was because we saw the tanks, the APCs, and anti-aircraft artillery along the asphalt road Prizren-Gjakove. At around 5.00, the Serbs from the village communicated with the army and the police, and fire was opened from the lower part. They started to go into the Albanian houses, the policemen, and to set the Albanian houses on fire, those that were along the main road. So when we saw this, we become scared. We left our houses and took to the mountains, to the woods near the creek. On the 25th of March, they were shelling from below, but none of the shells hit the location where the population was. We left our houses because of fear. That's why almost the entire population, about 400 or 500 villagers, got together and went to the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned the figure, 400 to 500 villagers. Even if it's only 400, it's a fairly large number. How did you get organised? How were you able to head in a specific direction in such a short time? Was there some kind of a previous agreement, a contingency agreement in case something like this happens? Did you expect something of the sort to happen?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There was no organisation per se. As I said, the main road, Gjakove-Prizren, was full of tanks and APCs, full of policemen and military personnel. When the policemen went to the houses, they set them on fire; and because of fear, the population left their houses, and we got together, all of us, there in the woods near the creek. This was not an organisation. We all left because of fear. It's not that we organised this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is about the place where you set off. That's your village, Mala Krusa. You headed into the woods towards the creek, which is fairly long, and the vineyards. How far is it from the village? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I think I marked it on the map. It's not very far. It doesn't even have a name. It's just a creek. It's near the village in the woods. It's not far. I did not measure the distance, so I don't know how far that would be exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will not insist on you telling us how far that was since you told us that it was not far. My next question is this: Did you not feel safer in your homes than in this area, which is completely open and unsheltered, and there was such a huge mass of people there?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We didn't feel safer in our homes because they entered the houses immediately. Those who didn't leave the houses, those nine persons that I mentioned, were burnt in their houses, and that's why we left, because we could well observe what was going on and what the police was doing in the village. We left because of fear, not because of our own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is this: Did somebody -- I'm not sure whether I understood the interpreter correctly. He said: "We didn't leave out of fear. We left of our own free will."

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There was a correction. That's why I'm not asking you this question. I withdraw the question. Now, did anyone tell you that you should or that you had to go into the woods?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No. We left because of fear. Nobody told us to go to the woods. When they began to open fire, there was -- it was no longer possible for us to remain in our homes. We had to leave our houses and seek shelter. We followed each other to the woods, the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already told us all this. Now, in order to save your time and because of judicial economy, as it is called, could you please answer my questions directly and not repeat what you've already said. Now, my next question is: Is it correct that none of the Serbs told you, Go into the woods, you have to go into the woods?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We didn't speak with the Serbs at that moment. They were busy setting the houses on fire. They were shelling. They were opening fire. How could we possibly talk to them? We left because of fear, not for pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I fully understand you. Thank you for your answer. My next question, Mr. Lutfi, is this: You got so scared. What was the reason, then, that as early as that night you went back and spent -- spent the night in your neighbour's home - you mentioned his name, but I'm not going to mention it - if your fear was really real and had foundations?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We returned to this neighbour's house because it was very cold. I already mentioned it. There were children, elderly, women, men there. It was very cold, and because of the cold we went to Sejdi Batusha's house. It's in the peripheral part of the village. It's in the outskirts, not inside the village, and we went the night there. We went there because it was cold, and mostly for the children; it was cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you do that of your own free will? I'm talking about your return back to the village, to the house of your neighbour.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We had to. It wasn't our free will. It was very cold, and we needed a roof on our heads. It was cold. We left our houses early in the morning. Most of the people were unable to get any warm clothes with them or food with them. We were completely unprepared when we left our houses. That's why we didn't have warm clothes with us, and in that cold temperature we could barely stay outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lutfi, you will agree with me, then, that the Serb police did not go into the woods with its forces and forced you out of the woods into your neighbour's yard where you spent the night?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The police were standing on the side. They didn't came to the location in the woods where we were near the creek. The army, they were further down along the main road, and the police was not where the population was. I am speaking about the time when we were in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, while you were in the woods, did anyone open fire on you, on the people who had fled and who were gathered there? Were they firing at you?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Those that opened fire were down there. The projectiles would go to the woods, to the hills. It would pass us over, and they would fall in the vineyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, please tell us, how far is this hill from the location where the people who had fled gathered? It was above you.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I'm not able to tell you exactly. Here was the creek, and the vineyards were a little bit above us, and the projectiles would fall there in the vineyards. I would say about 100 metres, 200 metres was the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ramadani, can you tell me, do you know the following persons whose names I will now tell you, and if you can tell me, please, who these persons are: Brahim Batusha, Arbin Hajdari, Avni Hajdari, Jeton Hajdari, Mehmet Shehu.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. These people are from my village. Jeton Hajdari and Mehmet, their houses are a little bit further, below the -- on the other side of the asphalt road, and they survived the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, do you know that these persons were members of the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I am not aware of any KLA members being present there, but everything is possible. I have not even heard about KLA presence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please answer me: From the village, and by that I mean the part of the village where you lived, where the houses are, where you spent the night, and I'm also referring to the place where this massacre happened, so from those locations, were you able to see the length of the asphalt road that links Prizren and Djakovica which passes through your village, to one side of it?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: You mean from my house? You can see everything from my house, the main road, Prizren-Gjakove included. From the area where we were, at Sejdi Batusha's house, you cannot see it very well. You have to go to the top floors of the house if you want to see the main road clearly, while you can see the road very well from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you could see that road from your house very well. The whole road or just parts thereof? Let us be very specific about it.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The road from our village towards Xerxe, the whole main road Prizren-Gjakove, you can see it very well. So the road Krusha e Vogel, Krusha e Madhe, Xerxe, and Celine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, could you please tell me, from the house where you sought shelter on that night, the 25th of March, to your house you told us the distance, the approximate distance in your testimony so far. I will not be asking you this. It's very close, but is there an elevation between your house and the road linking Prizren and Djakovica, a hill?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There isn't any hill in between. My house is on an elevation, and you can see the main road which is down there very well, but there is no hill in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And from the yard of the house where you sought shelter in the evening of the 25th, the Batusha house where you sought shelter for the night?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There is no hill between the road and that house either, but there are houses, other houses in between, and that's why you cannot see the main house clearly. You have to go to the top floors to see it. There are houses in between, up to the main road, and that's why you cannot see it clearly from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the military did not enter the village at all?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I didn't see soldiers in the village. I only saw soldiers around the village. The army was around the village by -- along the main road and on the hills, while the police were inside the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lutfi, you told us -- you described for us the fact that some local police were in the village, maybe reserve police officers who were recruited into the police force in your village. You mentioned their names. I will not be asking you any other questions about them, but you mentioned that some people had arrived, people who worked in the police in Prizren. Did you mention those people because you know them by sight or in any other way, or did you merely say that those people came from Prizren, or were those police officers from Prizren?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They were policemen who came from Prizren on a Pinzgauer, police officers. They were not locals. They were police officers. They were brought on Pinzgauers. They were left behind. The other lot were put into the Pinzgauers and deployed elsewhere. I have no idea where. The locals, that is, from Krusha e Vogel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about those who would come from Prizren? Did you know them, perhaps? Had you seen them in Prizren, or did you not know them at all?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't know them. They were policemen. I did not know them personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, in several of your statements and the several testimonies that you gave in the Milosevic case and the Milutinovic et al. case, you referred to something that you called paramilitary formations. Can you explain to us what it is that you meant when you said paramilitary formations, of the police, that is? As far as I understood you, that is; of course, you can correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I don't think I have ever mentioned paramilitaries. I don't think so. I've only talked about the police and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to find the reference by the end of this cross-examination, but let us not waste any time now. Let us move on to my next question. Today, you said several times that Serb forces shelled your village and the positions there. Did I understand you correctly that you had said there was shelling, or did you misspeak?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. They kept shooting from the main highway. They kept shooting towards the houses. Yes, there was shooting. I don't know whether that was shelling or what, but there was shooting, on the part of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask to have the witness's statement of the 5th of October, 2001, put on the monitor. It was given to investigator Pete Stewart. D001-4382. That's the English version, and in the Albanian language - could we please have both on the screens at the same time - D001-4392. It is page 2 -- I beg your pardon. Page 3, actually.
