We are looking at the paragraphs that are in the lower third of that page. I'm saying that because I'm now going to read out from part of the witness's statement, the statement of the witness who is being heard today. I'm going to ask him to explain the differences between the statement that he gave then and what he said today. The witness says as follows in that statement: "I saw 40 to 50 vehicles parked on the road." And then he says: "The vehicles that I saw were a mixture of APCs and Pragas. They were not camouflage." Next paragraph: "The APCs were normal blue colour MUP, and the Pragas were the normal VJ green. "The Pragas were armed with machine-guns and cannons. With Pragas, you can have different kind of weapons. The Pragas were manned by members of the Army of Yugoslavia. "I don't know who was manning the APCs, but I presume it was the MUP." This is a reference to the police. "I have been asked if I'm aware of any T55 tanks being stationed in the area of Krusha e Vogel at this time." The witness's answer is: "No." "I have been asked if I saw any rockets on any of these vehicles." The answer was: "No." "They asked me whether any one of these weapons had been used in the attack at Mala Krusa." And the witness says: "Yes. That happened on the 20th of March, 1999, at 4.30 in the morning, and it is bullets that hit the house walls that afflicted the only injury. Artillery was not used in this attack." Mr. Lutfi, I'm putting this to you so that you would tell us first and foremost why you stated something different today, and in this statement of the 5th of October, 2001, you said this, what I put to you just now. That would be my first question. However, we are going to be dealing with another part of your statement, as well, may I say that straightaway, what you said in the Milosevic trial. But could you please first respond to this.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The Pragas in their -- had the -- exactly the same colour they used to have before. They could have changed them. Whether there was any shelling from the Pragas or from rockets and so on, I don't think so. I have not seen any rockets shooting. They shot with cannons -- they were equipped with cannons, and they shot towards the houses. I don't know what they shot from. I don't know whether they used the cannons or whether they used automatic rifles or whether they used machine-guns, because they did have everything. They had cannons. They had automatic weapons, rifles, and machine-guns too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ramadani, was there shelling or was there not any shelling? In the statement you say there was no shelling, and you say that the only damage came from bullets. So was there any shelling or was there not any shelling, and why did you say then that there was no shelling, and why are you saying today that there was shelling? It's a brief question.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, there was shooting towards the walls of the houses, but I don't think heavy artillery was used. It was light weaponry. I don't think heavy artillery was used. That's what is written over there, and that's the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, you said several times today that the -- that the village had been shelled, and we all know what that means. That's why I'm asking you yet again why you said that today, if you will or if you wish to answer this question. Otherwise, I'm going to take your testimony the way you're giving it.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I'm saying today exactly what I said at that time, and I clarified by saying that there was shooting towards the walls of the houses. There was shooting, but it was not shooting that came from heavy weaponry, from artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So we can agree that there wasn't any shelling?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There was shelling, but it was not artillery shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I am satisfied with your answer, so I'm not going to put what it was that you stated in the Milutinovic case and what you stated in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to have this part of the statement admitted into evidence. I am not going to deal with what the witness had stated in the Milosevic case and the Milutinovic case in relation to the shelling of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The transcript of the witness, do you have particular page numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask to have page 3 admitted, from paragraph 6 up until the end, on page 3, that is. So that would include all of page 4 too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are we talking about transcript in the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. No. I'm talking about the witness statement. I gave you the D number. It's not going to be a problem for me to repeat this reference, Your Honour. This is a statement that was given to the investigators on the 5th of October, 2001. In English, it is D001-4382; and in Albanian, it is D001-4392. Just a moment, please. The witness statement -- actually, as I've already said, it is page 3 of the witness statement, and I'll tell you straightaway from what paragraph onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My request for page numbers is because I thought you were dealing with --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three, 3, page 3. Page 3 from paragraph 6 up until the end of the witness's statement. That means that page 4 should be included, too, so that it wouldn't seem that this portion was being taken out of context. So I'm speaking of the English version, from paragraph 6 on page 3 up until the end of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, that I asked for page numbers when I wrongly thought you were dealing with the transcript of the Milosevic and Milutinovic cases. I now understand what you're intending, and I think it will probably be easier simply to receive the past statement. Now, the statement that is on our screens, is that the one that you are tendering, the statement of the 5th of October, 2001?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, yes. And I will agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will receive that statement of the 5th of October, 2001, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00029, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we also have transcripts from the Milutinovic case and the Milosevic case. I'm not going to deal with them because I'm satisfied with the answer that I got from the witness after I showed him his witness statement. So we're not going to spend any more time on this. I would like to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, first of all, I would like to ask to show on the screens part of the witness's statement in the Milutinovic case. Actually, it is page 4285, and the Defence Exhibit is -- just a moment, please. I just need assistance. P00306. It is page 3. Right. It has to do with uniforms, Mr. Ramadani. We will have to dwell on that a bit longer because of what you stated to my learned friend who conducted your direct examination. In the Milutinovic case, you stated that the police wore black uniforms. Today, you say that the police wore blue uniforms. In certain statements, like the one that was already admitted into evidence, you say that this same police wore camouflage blue uniforms. So I would like to ask you - this is really important to ask -- well, we know what these people did, and we know what you feel, that it's -- that it's not important what these people wore but what they did, and I agree with that. But could you please tell us, why are you saying in Milutinovic black uniforms why? Do you say blue uniforms today? Why do you say on the 5th of October in this statement that I put to you this -- about the artillery, you're saying blue again, but this time blue camouflage uniforms? Could you please explain that to the Trial Chamber and to all of this -- to all of us so that we would know what this is all about?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I think there's been some misunderstanding. This one which I'm pointing to is black, and the blue that I mentioned is slightly -- a slightly lighter shade than this one, and you're saying not black and neither blue. I'm saying it's neither too black, nor too blue. I don't know whether you're able to understand me or not. It is not light blue; it's dark blue, navy blue. That is the uniforms they used to wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What you're saying today, dark blue. Today you're saying dark blue, and --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: And that's exactly what's written on the statement, blue. That's what the statement says. However, I'm not able to read this now because the letters are too small, but that's what the statement says. You can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I would kindly ask to have that same page returned on our screens from the witness's statement of October 5th, in Albanian, please, and in English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You want Exhibit D29.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You're saying, and that's page 3 -- I'm looking at the B/C/S version now. I'm going to check the English now. English, again, is paragraph 3 on page 3. "For example, Nebojsa Nikolic was a MUP reservist, and he was wearing a green camouflage uniform." You will admit that that is quite different from dark blue. So that's what you're saying about Nebojsa Nikolic, green camouflage uniform. Also, you say - 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 - here it is, the fifth paragraph, that they wore green camouflage uniforms as they were by the asphalt road, and you think that it's the VJ, and here we see that a member of the MUP is wearing green camouflage. Could you explain this to us a bit so that we would know who the members of these detachments are, who attacked the village, and who did what you said they did.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The ones who attacked the village were policemen. Nebojsa Nikolic was a young man, whilst the uniforms were of various colours. There were uniforms that were green, there were others that were blue, and they kept changing them. Sometimes they wore the blue, sometimes the green ones. There were others in the village who wore no uniforms at all, amongst the Serbs, that is, but they were -- they had their own weapons. They were armed. There were some policemen, local policemen from the local militia who had green uniforms. They'd change their uniforms. One day they wore them; another day they took them off. Yes. There were all kinds of uniforms. There were green. There were blue. They kept changing them. I don't think they attached great importance to that. Nebojsa eventually went to Pastrik, to Koshare, where he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question, it has to do with this particular reference that I said that I would go back to in order not to waste time. It has to do with when you mentioned paramilitary formations directly. You do it in the Milutinovic transcript. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I don't think I've mentioned the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 0306 is the transcript number, and page 40 is what we're looking at, lines 9 and 10. Could the usher please have this portion of the transcript displayed, from Milutinovic, that is, when the witness testified there, and when he refers to paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So please look at that page. It is zoomed in now, and I think you'll be able to read it. It is lines 9 and 10 of page 40. You say "paramilitary." Now, was -- is this something that you mentioned by chance or by mistake - because you said that you never said this - or is this perhaps, Mr. Lutfi, something that you forgot and that you remembered now and that you can explain to us now?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: It is not true that I used the word "paramilitary." I only spoke about police. I'm not aware of having used the word "paramilitary." I referred to the police and the army. The army did not enter the village. They stayed at a distance on the outskirts. The police did. I have not seen any paramilitaries. I'm not sure there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to ask you about that any more, then. Tell me, Suka Brdo, this hill, where is it in relation to your house and your village?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There is no Kodra Shuka in this village. I think this is a great mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever mention this name?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Never. Never, because it doesn't exist. There is no Kodra Shuka in the vicinity. I've never heard of one. It could be the Suka Brdo hill, but there is no such thing called Kodra Shuka. It's mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Suka Brdo? I'm saying this because I'm reading this from the Milutinovic transcript. It is page 4348. In e-court I don't know what the number is, but I'm sure the usher will find it, after all. It is lines 13 and 14. It says Suka, S-u-k-a. That's the name of the hill. You say that there is no such hill, but it's here in your answer, you know. So you say that you cannot see the asphalt road from this house but that you can see Shuka Brdo or Suka Brdo or something along those lines. So perhaps we should clarify this because these words are ascribed to you, you see, so if this is incorrect, we would like to have it corrected. It is -- it is the part of your testimony that is the cross-examination by my learned friend Mr. Visnjic in that trial.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There is no such hill. There is a hill called the Suka Brdo. It's at a distance, and there is no road leading to it. There isn't any other. There is no Shuka there, nowhere in that area that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us slowly what the exact name of the hill is. So there is no such thing as Shuka Brdo or Suka Brdo; right?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Suka Brdo. That is at a fair distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Suka Brdo, what is that?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Just an elevated piece of land.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you mean when you said that from Suka Brdo - now I understand what you mean - that from there you can see the asphalt road? Where is it in relation to the village, and where is it in relation to the road, so where? Where is it? You say it was far away. Is it south? North? Just explain that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It's northwards like this, and I don't know what the point is of this Suka Brdo. There never happened anything over there. It never interested me. I don't think I ever mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I've just showed you the transcript where you mentioned this, but it wasn't "Saka." It says "Suka Brdo" over here. Could you please tell me where you were on the 13th of May and where you were on the 2nd of June, 1999? So first the 13th of May and then on the 2nd of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: On the 13th of May, I was up in the mountains. I had escaped. I just survived the massacre, whereas the others from the family, the women, they were in Albania. They were taken all the way to Albania whilst I was roaming around the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were you close to the village or far away from it? You were -- you mentioned mountains.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Beyond the Drin River, Drini i Bardhe. Roaming the mountains, that's where I was. From -- we could -- we were on the other side. We could see -- we could see the asphalt road and -- and the village. We were, but we were at a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, do you remember the NATO air-strikes in Mala Krusa on the 13th of May?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it. I -- we saw the aeroplanes over flying. I don't think there was any bombing in that area at all. We could see the aircraft flying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear any explosions on the 13th of May?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I did not hear any explosions in that area. I don't think there was any. All we could see is the aeroplanes flying. I don't think there was any bombing in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that, or are you claiming that with full certainty?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I think I'm certain there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The 2nd of June, 1999, where were you then?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I was in Albania on the 2nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that on that day your village was bombed by NATO, or is it something that you don't know about?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No, I don't know about it. I was in Albania, and I could not see or hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lutfi, let me now move on to the set of questions that will have to do with the list of people who were set on fire in the barn, as you described it. Do you know Mr. Mehmet Krasniqi, also known as Mehmet Avdyli or Krasniqi? Do you know why Mr. Krasniqi changed his name?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: He was traumatised at the time. He was burnt and probably not in a state to remember or tell his name, and he could not even write it down because his hands were burnt. I was also burnt on the right-hand side. It's the same person, Mehmet Krasniqi, or Mehmet Avdyli. It's the same person. He's my neighbor. He's from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that for a fact, that that's why he changed his last name, or is it just an assumption on your part?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: He was burnt, as I said. He was traumatised. He was not fully conscious. He gave his statement when he arrived at Kukes in the capacity of Mehmet Avdyli, but his name -- full name is Mehmet Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Ramadani, you said today: "We made a list of people who were burnt in this massacre, who were killed." Did I understand you correctly when you say "we made the list..." or is it that you yourself did it, or if you did it with somebody else, who assisted you in reconstructing the whole event? Who were those people, if there were any.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: It's the same people we're talking about, regardless of whether I compiled the list on my own or with the help of a neighbour or another person. One hundred and three persons were killed and burned in the barn. Nine persons who refused to leave their houses were burnt in their houses. Krusha e Vogel has 800 inhabitants; 112 people were executed and burnt. I was among these men. My sons were there too. I survived; they didn't. I have all their names, surnames, dates of birth. I might be mistaken for a year or two as regards their year of birth, and I have pictures of them with me here, and I can show them to you if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, it's very difficult for me to ask you questions and to try in any way, including this way, to traumatise you by making you remember some things, but I would just like to ask you one question regarding this list. I merely wanted to find out something that is logical to me. Is it true that you made this list together with the villagers from your village, because there were many people, 103, and then you have to make an effort to recall all their names and dates of birth. I don't have anything against that, but I would like to get a logical explanation. So did you make this list together with people from your village? Were there several of you? How did you -- all of you make this list?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I was on my own. We were in Sejdi Batusha's house and near the creek together with all these men that were killed. We were at the location where we were forming columns of three. I knew all their names maybe with the exception of a -- younger people, of some youths whose dates of birth I didn't know, and then a neighbour helped me with dates of birth. As for the names and last names, I knew all of them myself, because they were from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer, Mr. Ramadani. My next question is: Did you get acquainted with the list that was provided to this Tribunal through the OTP investigators by Mehmet Avdyli Krasniqi, whom we mentioned? Do you know what list he made or had?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The list we are talking about is my list, the list that I compiled. Nobody gave me the list. I might have given the list to others, but nobody gave a list to me. There were people who were disabled amongst those killed. I compiled the list myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that quite -- in some detail. I'm asking you this because there are some discrepancies. The only thing that is the same is the total number of persons who were killed. You both claim that 103 villagers were killed, but I looked at the lists, and I noticed some discrepancies. This is why I'm asking you this. Now I have to ask you yet another question. From that day when you fled from the execution site at this -- from this barn in Batusha, were any bodies of the victims who were killed there found ever? Their mortal remains, were they found?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No. They were burnt. They were all ashes. The Serbs from the village, they removed the ashes and threw them in the Drini River. When we returned from Albania, all we could see left from the site were these two craters and nothing else, the concrete blocks scattered in the meadows as a result the explosion, nothing else. I didn't go to the Drini River to have a look. They asked me to go, but I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now I will ask you -- well, it's a problem now because I have the daily transcript of the evidence of Mehmet Krasniqi. That's page 1009. That's from Friday, the 13th of February, lines, 19, 20, and 21. If we could please have that shown by the court deputy or the usher. My assistant is trying to find this portion, but we can't get at this part of the transcript in e-court, but if the Chamber will allow me to put it to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- what Mr. Krasniqi said on that occasion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The witness says: "[In English] They are all dead, the remaining persons on that list. Only 20 bodies were identified and buried in our village. The remaining victims, we don't know where they are. We never found their remains." [Interpretation] Then at page 1065 of the daily transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you move on, perhaps you could just put to the witness, does he know of anything of some 20 bodies being identified and buried?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, precisely what you've just said is the logical sequence. This is what I wanted to do. So my question to the witness is this: First, I wanted to put both to him and to the Trial Chamber -- or to explain to the witness why I'm going to ask him that, and then I want to elicit from the witness whether he knew anything about that, since I received an answer to a question asked of Mr. Mehmet in cross-examination that some 20 bodies were identified and buried, and now I want to ask him anything about that, and then I intended to ask some more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Those that were burned in their houses, we found upon returning to the village after the war their remains. Some -- it is said that some bodies have been identified, but personally I don't believe it because we're talking about ashes here that was brought to the morgue in Prishtina. The only material that these victims could be identified from were these ashes. To this date, I don't know anything about the remains or the ashes of my two sons. So that's why I'm quite pessimistic. This is -- these are the bodies that Mehmet Avdyli spoke about. It is true that there are 20 graves in our village, the graves of these 20 victims. As for others, nothing has changed to this date. We don't know anything about their remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It is quite obvious that you have no knowledge of that, so I will not be asking you any more questions about this, but let me tell you once again, I asked a direct question whether these were people who were killed in the barn, in the same place where you claim the massacre happened, and Mr. Mehmet said those were the people and that as for the rest, their fate remains unknown to this day. Mr. Lutfi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you go on, Mr. Djordjevic, we need to have that second break now if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Judge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we will resume, then, at 20 minutes past.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Since we're waiting, can I just use the opportunity to indicate that we have received indication from the victims and witnesses unit that the next witness slated as K90 is very ill and will not be available to testify on Wednesday. So we -- subject to the Court, with leave of the Court, we ask that we call Nike Peraj before him, to reverse the schedule with those two witnesses and call K90 on Friday if he recovers, if the victim and witnesses unit indicates that we can proceed, and, of course, subject to what my friend has to say about it. I was going to mention this at the end of the proceedings, but I arose because of the interrignum. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there a problem, Mr. Djordjevic, with that reversal?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This kind of a change certainly is a serious difficulty for us due to the pace of our preparations in this case because Mr. Djurdjic and I have absolutely prepared to work on preparing for Witness K90. So we thought that we could be hearing Mr. Peraj on Friday or Monday at the earliest. So the Defence is not prepared to hear Mr. Peraj on Wednesday. Your Honours, to be perfectly honest about this, we cannot handle it before Friday if we really want to be sure that our client has the right to a fair defence. We have really been working very hard on K90. We understand the Prosecutor's reasons, but we really cannot start Peraj on Wednesday. So, Your Honour, we cannot do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is grateful for your indication, Mr. Stamp, and it is conscious of the concerns of Mr. Djordjevic. In the Chamber's view, at this stage we would take the view that we should hear the evidence in chief of Witness K90 on Wednesday. If at the end of the evidence in chief Defence counsel is able to deal with some issues, we will proceed with that. Failing that, cross-examination will be on Friday of K90 -- I beg your pardon, of Mr. Peraj. And if at the end of the evidence of Mr. Peraj the witness has recovered, we will move to Witness K90. What this circumstance has disclosed is a difficulty about which we will make specific directions later, but the important thing at the moment is to move on in the hope of finishing this witness tonight, so we will not delay now. So if you can continue, then, Mr. Djordjevic, with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Your Honours, may I say that I agree that we can start with the direct on Wednesday, no problem with that, if Mr. Stamp can handle it. I'm not opposed to that at all. I would now like to continue straightaway with my cross-examination of this witness. Could we please have on our screens now P312. That's a list that was created by this witness. I just have one question in relation to the list. Could we please have page 4. Page 4, please. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, in the second column are the persons who you listed as persons who were found in their own houses and were burned or lost their lives in another way. So these are Sali Shehu, Dervish Shehu, and Nexhat Shehu, Sejdi Emerllahu, Nazmi Rashkaj, Demir Rashkaj, and then you added Isnija Rashkaj. We see that this is a total of nine persons. You said now unequivocally that there are 20 mounds in the village. Can you tell us about the remaining 11. If this has to do with what you said, I can infer that these nine persons were buried at the same cemetery. So there are 11 remaining mounds or tombs, and you haven't told us who they belong to. So this is a brief question. If we could have a brief comment from you.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The other people were not the ones who were buried there, whilst these ones on the list were the ones burnt to death in their own houses; whilst as regards the others, we have a common grave. We left them in the same common grave. However, later identification was made possible. They exhumed the ashes. They were able to make the identification, which then resulted in the burial in individual graves, those people who were able to be identified. So they were identified, they were given their own names, and they were buried individually. As far as I'm concerned, this is not that significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ramadani, can we conclude that you are stating with certainty that none of these persons who were killed in the massacre that had to do with the barn or the Batusha family were buried here? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, they are. I didn't say that. There are nine who were in their own homes, and we -- I wasn't part of the party that went to retrieve the ashes from the Drin River, and they were able to make the identification based exactly on the ashes. So they were able to identify 11 from the ashes. This is why identification was made possible, which then resulted in their burial. The ashes were retrieved from the Drin River.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, Mr. Ramadani, that it is impossible to get ashes out of a river. Are these remains of a skeleton of a victim, or what is it that you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: When they went to the river, they were able to collect ashes and the occasional bone that remained. They put everything in their proper bags, and then they were able to make the identifications. I will -- I was not with them when this happened. They called me. They invited me to go, but I refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ramadani, we can conclude that you are claiming nevertheless that these are the remains of the persons who were massacred in the barn of the Batusha family; right?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. The ashes come from the barn that belongs to Qazim Batusha, whereas when it concerns the others who were burned in their own house, the occasional remains were found in the houses to make the identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Ramadani, when were these remains found on the banks of the Drim River? When did that happen? What year was that?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Immediately after we returned from Albania, two or three weeks afterwards, not any more. It was in the month of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani -- would you like to say something else, actually?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No. What I was going to say is upon returning from Albania, this happened. I cannot recall the exact date. I never noted it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I wanted to ask you. I wanted to ask you, and I did ask you, about the approximate time. My next question: Do you know how the bodies were identified, or, rather, who was it that identified these remains? What forensic team, because this requires a great deal of professional skill.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there. Forgive me. They are professionals. I don't know. I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My last question in relation to this, Mr. Ramadani: You're not the only witness and the only survivor of this massacre, as we've been calling it. How is it possible that today no one said this? This is the first time we hear of this, and the massacre took place almost ten years ago. No witness ever said it. No prosecutor ever said it. You never said it. No one else did.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I think I did say. This statement does not come from today. It's from a long time ago. It is not that I write this statement now. I wrote it immediately after the war, immediately after returning from Albania. I gave the statement at that stage as well as compiling the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is, indeed, not contained in any one of your statements, but I'm not going to ask you anything else about this. I'm going to go back to the crime scene. Mr. Lutfi, you said several times in your statements that the site was blown up. Could you please tell me on the basis of what you actually said that?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I can say -- I can say that it was an explosion because there are only two craters. Everything has been uprooted. The only thing that exists over there at the moment is two craters that are filled with either grass or water. That's why I say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, you mentioned in your testimony a bulldozer. Could you please tell me in what context this bulldozer was mentioned as far as the crime scene was concerned? Who was it that saw these bulldozers on the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: If I recall it correctly, I did not mention it. However, the tracks were visible when we returned. I'm not sure I've ever mentioned that or who was with that bulldozer at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nilsen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution would like know which pages of the testimony the Defence lawyer is referring to when he's calling upon the mentioned bulldozers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is my recollection that there was no reference to bulldozers in the evidence of the witness, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm quite sure that this was mentioned. I will go back to the reference as I did a few moments ago when we were dealing with paramilitaries. I will go back to the reference to bulldozers. They were mentioned, for sure, but I'd like to move on now because time is precious. I had assumed that the witness is going to say something in line with what he had already stated, but that obviously did not happen. Now could we have P311 displayed. So there is a wheelchair. I think Sait Hajdari was mentioned by the witness. So could we please see this on the screen now. Yes. Now we have the image.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: After displaying this image, I would like to ask the witness whether it is with certainty that he recognises Hajdari's wheelchair and the wife of the late Sait Hajdari. Could the witness please have a careful look.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm certain that this is Sait Hajdari's wheelchair. Two hundred per cent certain, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And what about his wife? Do you recognise her with certainty?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: His wife, too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask the usher to display a portion of the Milutinovic transcript, P00306, page 9, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In line 16, when you are asked whether that was the wheelchair and whether you can compare it to the wheelchair that actually had to do with what happened in 1999, you say that it is similar. You are now saying that it's Sait Hajdari's wheelchair. Why did you state that then, and why do you say you are 100 or 200 per cent sure? Could you just tell me that?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I'm absolutely certain that that was Sait Hajdari's wheelchair. I said it at the time, and I'm saying it today, that that wheelchair belonged to Sait Hajdari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The reference you made is not the one that's on the screen, I'm afraid, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'm just a little bit tired, but it is -- I'm positive that it is not Milutinovic. It is Milosevic, in fact, testimony. D0014430, page 9. That's the right reference. [Interpretation] The witness then said that the wheelchair was similar. He did not speak with any degree of certainty. So it's not true that he said then what he's saying now. Secondly, in response to the direct question as to whether he knew the woman on the photograph, that's already on line -- in line 4 of the next page, he says, "No, I do not know this woman." How does the witness know the woman now and did not know her then? How can his memory be better now than it was then at that time? Could he just explain that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, this is now the transcript on the screen, isn't it? Line 9: "You referred to a wheelchair being positioned in the doorway..." et cetera. Is that the one that you mentioned? And the answer at line 16, the answer: "It's similar."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, if you go on to line 17 and 18: "Who was the crippled individual in the wheelchair?" The answer is: "Sait Hajdari was in this wheelchair." Then at line 19: "Do you recognise the lady depicted in that photograph?" Yes -- At line 25: "Yes, I know this person. I knew ..." and it's on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not right, Your Honour. Witness thought about Hajdari Sait, but look at the next page, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Is that correct, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're waiting for the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's not the next page that's come on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It's page number 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the first answer is that it's "Sait Hajdari, and that's what his wheelchair was like." And then the question is asked: "Do you know the lady ..." "No, I don't know this woman." "Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, I think that what you put to the witness is not correct. What emerges from this evidence is that this is similar to, or this is what the wheelchair was like, but it was the wheelchair in which Sait Hajdari was sitting, and the lady with the wheelchair on this evidence is, "No, I don't know this woman." I think you suggested to the witness that he couldn't identify the wheelchair and he couldn't identify the lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not want to put anything to the witness, although leading questions are allowed in the cross-examination. What I wanted to ask this witness is why at that time he stated that the wheelchair was similar, and that's what he did say, that Sait Hajdari was a person in a wheelchair, and that's not controversial at all. But when he was asked about the wheelchair, he said it was similar, he wasn't 100 per cent sure, and when he was asked by the Prosecution whether he knew the woman, he said, "No, I don't know this woman." And when it was clarified to him -- that's why I want to ask the witness why we have this discrepancy in his evidence between what he said then and what he's saying now. How come that today he's 100 per cent sure that this is the wheelchair and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Mr. Ramadani, you have seen, I believe, a transcript of your evidence in the trial of Mr. Milosevic when you were shown, I believe, the same photograph as is now Exhibit P311, the lady and the wheelchair, and you said that you did not know this woman. In your evidence today, you've indicated that although you didn't know her well, you're sure that that is the wife of Sait Hajdari. Are you able to offer any explanation for the difference in your evidence on these two occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is not important as far as this lady's concerned, whether she was Sait's wife or not. The important thing is that this wheelchair belongs to Sait Hajdari and that he was seated in it and that the wheelchair was placed at the doorway. At the time, I didn't take any interest in knowing this woman. That was not important to me, and this might be the difference that the gentleman is pointing out, whether I said that this was the woman or that she was not the woman. The important thing for me, at least, is that this is the wheelchair that belonged to Sait and that Sait was seated in it when he was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is your evidence today that the woman in the photograph is the wife of Sait Hajdari evidence that you are now certain about, or are you saying that you do not know that woman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm certain that this is his wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And do you have any explanation why you did not know that when you gave evidence in the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I didn't have any contacts. I didn't see that woman. I knew that Sait was disabled, couldn't move. She would take him out for a walk. I didn't take any interest in knowing her. When we returned, however, after the war from Albania, I got to know her and found out who she was. This is the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I have concentrated on the lady in the photograph because the evidence of the witness about that is clearly in contradiction. I think the evidence about the actual wheelchair is less clear, but you see where we have got about the identification of the woman, and I hope that has assisted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Unfortunately, I have to say that I am unable to complete the cross-examination of this witness today. I will have to continue into the next trial day, and I have a set of questions that will take 20 minutes or so. It's a logical hole, so I would like us to stop working now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Fortunately, Mr. Djordjevic, it is possible for the Chamber now to sit tomorrow morning. A courtroom is available. It hadn't been, but it is now the case, so that it will be possible for us to continue tomorrow morning to conclude the evidence of this witness, I would expect in the first session, which will mean that at least this witness will be able to leave, and we can then proceed with the evidence in chief of the next witness commencing Wednesday morning. If there's no difficulty with either counsel about sitting tomorrow morning to finish this witness - I see there is none - that is what the Chamber will do. Mr. Ramadani, we must now adjourn for the evening. It's 7.00, but we have arranged to proceed to finish your evidence tomorrow morning. So we will sit again at 9.00, and we expect that your evidence will be concluded early in the day and you will be able to get away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's how it's going to be, Your Honour, I'm sure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of February, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.58 p.m.,
